title: Mapping-space pullback criterion and existence of finite coherent limits
statement:
Use quasicategories, spaces, coherent cones and their limiting property as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $\mathscr E$ be a quasicategory. An object $e$ is terminal exactly when $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,e)$ is weakly contractible for every $x$. A coherent square with vertices $p,a,b,c$, presenting a cone on $a\to c\leftarrow b$, is limiting exactly when its projection-induced comparison
$$\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,p)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,a)\times^h_{\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,c)}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,b)$$
is an equivalence of spaces for every $x$. Here, for maps $a:A\to C$ and $b:B\to C$ of Kan complexes, $A\times_C^h B$ denotes the space modeled by $A\times_{C,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,C)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,C}B$, whose points are triples $(u,v,\gamma)$ with a path $\gamma:a(u)\to b(v)$, retaining all higher simplices. The comparison retains the square's specified coherence. These criteria are invariant under equivalences of apices and of cospan diagrams, and the comparisons are natural in maps of cones. If $\mathscr E$ has a terminal object and a limiting cone on every cospan, then every diagram $K\to\mathscr E$ with $K$ a simplicial set having finitely many nondegenerate simplices has a limiting coherent cone; this is existence of finite limits.

source.place: Theorem 6.6.9 and Remark 6.6.11 (Yoneda/mapping-space criterion for a Cartesian square), Theorem 7.3.27 (finite limits from terminal objects and pullbacks). Online PDF read on 2026-10-17; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: Terminality is exactly the mapping-space condition by [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]: its word 'contractible' means weakly contractible, including nonemptiness. For later use set $E_F(x)=\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(K,\mathscr E)}(\Delta_Kx,F)$, the space of coherent cones with fixed apex $x$. The cone criterion of [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus] says that a specified cone $\lambda:\Delta_Kp\to F$ is limiting if and only if composition with it gives an equivalence $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,p)\to E_F(x)$ for every $x$. This criterion concerns the given transformation and all its higher data, rather than a set of compatible morphisms in the homotopy category.

proof.text: For maps $u:U\to W$ and $v:V\to W$ of Kan complexes, [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison] says exactly that the stated path pullback is Kan and that the constant-path inclusion from the strict pullback is a weak homotopy equivalence if either leg is a Kan fibration. This supplies both fibration cases with the required path orientation; no choice of a strict path-inversion operation is used.

proof.text: Strictly commuting objectwise weak equivalences of Kan-complex spans induce weak equivalences of the path models by [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-pullback-invariance]. For spans commuting by specified homotopies, apply [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-commuting-pullback-invariance]: its endpoint-path formula is the required comparison, with all parameter simplices retained. The coherent composition and inverse homotopies used in the formula are those of [lem-cbc-simplicial-composition-spine]. This extracts the homotopy-commuting and parameterized argument formerly carried inline.

proof.text: Let $K=B\amalg_A D$ with $A\hookrightarrow D$ degreewise injective, and let $F,G:K\to\mathscr E$. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-excision]. Its equivalence is the actual restriction-and-constant-path comparison on transformation mapping spaces, natural in both diagrams and compatible with coherent precomposition and postcomposition. Taking $F=\Delta_Kx$ computes the fixed-apex cone space $E_G(x)$ and preserves the actual maps induced by supplied cones. No limit or colimit existence in $\mathscr E$ is assumed.

source.place: Proposition 7.3.16, mapping-space calculation underlying gluing along a monomorphism; online text read 2026-10-17, not archived. Agent expansion through the cited elementary foundations.

proof.text: Every diagram $F:\Delta^n\to\mathscr E$ has a limiting cone at $F(0)$, natural in $F$: this is the opposite of the standard-simplex clause of [lem-coef-infinity-final-index-colimit]. To check conventions, replace an operator $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ by $i\mapsto n-\alpha(m-i)$. This involution exchanges inner horns with inner horns, reverses cones to cocones, and preserves finite nondegenerate-simplex counts. The mapping-space issue is handled by [lem-coef-infinity-pinch-comparison]: reversing the arrow prism identifies $U_{Q^{\mathrm{op}}}(a,b)$ with $U_Q(b,a)^{\mathrm{op}}$. Reversing barycentric coordinates gives a homeomorphism between the realizations of a simplicial set and its opposite, since it intertwines exactly the reversed operators. Contractibility and equivalences of these mapping spaces therefore agree. The standard-simplex cocone in the cited node consequently reverses to the initial-vertex limiting cone. By the cone criterion of step 1, evaluation of a cone at vertex $0$ identifies $E_F(x)$ with $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,F(0))$, up to its natural inverse, composition with this standard cone. In particular, for $F=(a\xrightarrow{f}c)$, the restriction to vertex $c$ is postcomposition by $f$; the cone's triangle supplies this equality up to its specified homotopy.

source.place: Theorem 6.4.5 specialized to the initial vertex of a standard simplex; finite-shape proof in Theorem 7.3.27; online text read 2026-10-17, not archived. Agent expansion through the cited elementary foundations.

proof.text: Write the cospan shape as the union of its two edges $J=\Delta^1_{a,c}\amalg_{\{c\}}\Delta^1_{b,c}$. Apply step 4 with $F$ there the constant diagram at $x$ and $G$ the given cospan. It identifies $E_G(x)$ with the path pullback of the two edge-cone spaces over $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,c)$. Step 5 identifies these edge-cone spaces with $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,a)$ and $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr E}(x,b)$; their maps to the common space are postcomposition with the cospan arrows. By step 3, this identifies $E_G(x)$ with exactly the path-pullback space displayed in the statement. To verify the comparison map, a cone from $p$ has legs to $a,c,b$ and the coherent triangles along the two edges. Precomposing its triangles by $x\to p$ gives paths between each composite and the middle leg; concatenate one with the inverse of the other to obtain the path from the composite through $a$ to the composite through $b$. This is the specified square coherence under the two edge-cone identifications. The prism restrictions of step 4 prove the same identity for all parameter simplices. Substituting this identification into the cone criterion of step 1 proves both directions of the pullback criterion.

source.place: Theorem 6.6.9 and Remark 6.6.11, Cartesian-square mapping-space criterion; online text read 2026-10-17, not archived. Agent expansion through the cited elementary foundations.

proof.text: The comparisons are natural in maps of cones: on any parameter simplex, they restrict the same prism to the two edges and concatenate its two compatibility paths as in step 6. Restriction commutes with every face and degeneracy, and composition respects the simplicial coherences of [lem-cbc-simplicial-composition-spine]. For invariance, an equivalence between apices induces homotopy equivalences on incoming mapping spaces by composing with its inverse and the inverse-triangle homotopies. An equivalence of cospan diagrams induces equivalences between the two coherent cone spaces $E_G(x)$: the inverse equivalence and its two natural homotopies can be composed in the functor quasicategory, which exists by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. The mapping-space criterion of step 1 is therefore preserved and reflected by two-out-of-three. Under the explicit identification of step 6 this is precisely invariance of the path-pullback test, retaining the square's coherence.

source.place: Theorem 6.6.9, functoriality of the actual cone comparison; online text read 2026-10-17, not archived. Agent expansion through the cited elementary foundations.

proof.text: For finite-limit existence we first spell out the gluing operation, rather than invoke the existing finite-shape theorem whose present dependency closure returns to this item. Suppose $K=B\amalg_A D$ with $A\hookrightarrow D$ monic, and a diagram $F:K\to\mathscr E$ has chosen limiting cones on $B,A,D$, with apices $X,Y,Z$. The cone criterion in [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus] induces maps $X\to Y$ and $Z\to Y$ with coherent identifications between their composed $A$-cones and the restrictions of the chosen $B,D$-cones. Indeed each restricted cone is a point of $E_{F|_A}(X)$ or $E_{F|_A}(Z)$; the equivalence from the relevant mapping space gives the map and a path to that point. These two maps form a cospan, which has a limiting cone with apex $P$ by the assumed pullback existence. Compose its legs with the $B,D$-cones. Their restrictions to $A$ are coherently identified by the pullback cone and the two chosen paths; hence they determine a point of $E_{F|_B}(P)\times^h_{E_{F|_A}(P)}E_{F|_D}(P)$. The equivalence of step 4 is surjective on components, so choose an actual cone $\lambda$ on $F$ whose restriction triple is joined to that point by a path. For every $x$, the local limiting cones and step 3 identify this path pullback of local cone spaces with $\operatorname{Map}(x,X)\times^h_{\operatorname{Map}(x,Y)}\operatorname{Map}(x,Z)$. Step 6 identifies the latter with $\operatorname{Map}(x,P)$, by the given pullback cone. The compatibility with composition proved in step 4 means that the composite equivalence is the map induced by $\lambda$, up to the chosen path. Step 1 therefore proves $\lambda$ limiting. No global limit existence or Yoneda theorem has been used in this construction.

source.place: Proposition 7.3.16, finite gluing of existing local limits; details for the actual coherent cone; online text read 2026-10-17, not archived. Agent expansion through the cited elementary foundations.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-infinity-monomorphism-boundary-cells] to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow K$, where $K$ has finitely many nondegenerate simplices. Its stages attach exactly the nondegenerate $n$-simplices along $\partial\Delta^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$. There are finitely many cells in total and a largest cell dimension if $K$ is nonempty. Within each stage, order its finite set of cells arbitrarily and attach them successively: this gives the same pushout, because maps out of either presentation are one map on the previous stage and one on each simplex, agreeing with the prescribed boundary maps. Thus $K$ is obtained from the empty shape by finitely many single-cell attachments. A boundary $\partial\Delta^n$ has as its nondegenerate simplices the injective proper ordinal maps to $[n]$, so is finite of dimension $<n$ (and is empty for $n=0$). All statements here concern nondegenerate simplices, not degreewise finiteness, and allow distinct faces of an attached simplex to become identified in $K$.

source.place: Lemma 7.3.26, finite simplicial cell induction; boundary-cell construction; online text read 2026-10-17, not archived. Agent expansion through the cited elementary foundations.

proof.text: Assume a terminal object and limiting cones on every cospan. Prove existence for all finite diagrams by induction on their dimension, with the empty diagram first, and within a dimension by induction on the number of top-dimensional cells. The empty diagram has a limiting cone by the assumed terminal object and the definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For an attachment $K=K_0\amalg_{\partial\Delta^n}\Delta^n$ of step 9, the restriction to $K_0$ has a limit by the inner induction, or by the outer induction if its dimension has dropped. The restriction to $\partial\Delta^n$ has a limit by the outer induction; for $n=0$ this is the terminal object. The restriction to $\Delta^n$ has its initial-vertex limit by step 5. The boundary inclusion into the simplex is a monomorphism, so step 8 glues these three limits using a pullback. This completes both inductions. For $n=0$ it constructs finite products by pullbacks over the terminal object, and higher attachments allow noninjective boundary attaching maps without alteration. The resulting cone is limiting in the prescribed coherent sense. This proves the last assertion for every simplicial set with finitely many nondegenerate simplices.
